title: Main dispute: are we formally justified by inherent justice?
source_text: XL. Quamvis autem in multis quae hactenus recensuimus, circa naturam & meri-tum justitiae, & sanctitatis quae regenitis inest, inter se consentiant Protestantes & Pontificii; inter eos tamen quaestio est magna contentione animorum agitata, An per justitiam quae nobis inhaeret formaliter coram Deo justificemur? quod affirmant Pontificii, post Concilium Tridentinum, Protestantes vero magno consensu negant. De cujus quaestionis statu atque momento, ut recte judicetur, necesse est partium con-tendentium mentem distinctius & clarius exponere.
pass_a_gloss: But although in many things which we have thus far recounted concerning the nature and desert of the righteousness and holiness that is in the regenerate Protestants and Papists agree among themselves, yet among them a question is agitated with great contention of minds: Whether we are formally justified before God by the righteousness that inheres in us?—which the Papists after the Council of Trent affirm, but the Protestants with great consent deny. That the state and moment of this question may be rightly judged, it is necessary to set forth more distinctly and clearly the mind of the contending parties.
pass_b_english: Despite much agreement on nature of regenerate holiness, a heated question remains: are we formally justified before God by inherent justice?
Rome after Trent says yes; Protestants with great consent say no—minds must be stated clearly.
